rows: Temporary works should be planned and managed as part of the construction process.
Design should account for foreseeable loads and stages of work.
Competent people should design, check and implement temporary works.
A temporary works coordinator can support effective control on relevant projects.
Design assumptions and limitations should be communicated to site teams.
Installation should follow the approved design and sequence.
Changes require controlled review rather than informal site modification.
Inspection and permission-to-load or dismantle should be defined where needed.
A drawing or coordinator appointment does not prove that temporary works are correctly installed.
Conclusions require design, checks, sequence, installation, loading, change control, inspection and sign-off evidence.
Construction sites need lighting suitable for safe access and work.
Lighting should cover routes, work areas, edges and changes in level.
Glare and deep shadow should be controlled.
Temporary lighting should be positioned and protected against damage.
Lighting supplies and fittings must be electrically safe.
Emergency or backup lighting may be needed where failure creates danger.
Lighting should reflect night work, weather and changing site layouts.
Defective lighting should be reported and corrected promptly.
A lighting plan or lamp count does not prove adequate visibility at the point of work.
Conclusions require measured conditions, task, route, glare, shadows, maintenance, supply and emergency evidence.
Construction work must be planned to protect members of the public.
Site boundaries should prevent unauthorised access.
Children and other vulnerable people require particular consideration.
Falling objects and debris must be contained or excluded from public areas.
Vehicle movements should be separated from pedestrians outside and at site entrances.
Scaffolds, ladders and plant should be secured against unauthorised use.
Public routes and neighbouring properties should be considered in the work plan.
Controls should remain effective outside working hours.
A fence or warning sign does not prove that public access is adequately controlled.
Conclusions require boundary, access, overhead hazards, traffic, security, timing, neighbours and inspection evidence.
Materials should be stored so they do not collapse, fall or create access hazards.
Storage areas should be planned for the type, quantity and movement of materials.
Stacks should be stable and within safe height and loading limits.
Cylindrical or rolling items should be restrained.
Flammable and hazardous materials require appropriate segregation and controls.
Routes, exits and fire equipment should remain unobstructed.
Waste should be removed or contained to prevent trips, fire and environmental hazards.
Storage conditions should be inspected as work and weather change.
A stock list or storage-zone marking does not prove that stacks are stable.
Conclusions require material, stack geometry, ground, restraint, segregation, handling, weather and inspection evidence.
